title: the Arthashastra's opening
tomorrow: crumbs on a pond. who eats first, and who stops them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Arthashastra's opening counted the sciences, let the rivals speak first, and gave reasoned inquiry the lamp. Today, the whole science gets a one-line summary.

A phone buzzes, face down on a nightstand. One buzz, and a whole body turns toward it. A smell from the kitchen does the same, or a song from a passing car. The Arthashastra, a handbook for kings, names that pull early on. Then it makes a claim that sounds out of place in a book about armies and treasuries. This whole science, it says, is victory over the senses.
screen: `ONE BUZZ, AND THE BODY TURNS.` → `A BOOK ABOUT ARMIES…` → `…SAYS IT'S ALL ABOUT THE SENSES.`

segments.voice: The phrase is indriya jaya, victory over the senses. The text says what it means: the ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue and the nose don't run wild after sound, touch, sight, taste and smell. Not shut down. Steered. Then it names what has to be given up: desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance and reckless glee. And it warns that a ruler who can't do this soon perishes, even if he holds the whole earth. Then, instead of a lecture, it tells on kings. Dandakya, of the Bhoja line, went after a brahmin's daughter, and was destroyed with his kingdom. Ravana, out of pride, would not give back another man's wife. Duryodhana would not give his cousins their share of the kingdom. Two names this path already knows, from the epics, turning up here as warnings in a handbook of government. The logic is plain. A ruler who can't govern his anger will govern a kingdom with it. One who can't govern his greed will tax with it. So the first territory a king has to win is the five doors of his own body. The throne makes bigger whatever sits on it.
screen: `INDRIYA JAYA: VICTORY OVER THE SENSES.` · `NOT SHUT DOWN. STEERED.` · `KINGS UNDONE BY ONE PULL EACH.` · `THE FIRST TERRITORY IS YOU.` · then, large: `THE THRONE MAKES IT BIGGER.`

segments.voice: Pick one sound around you: a fan, traffic, a clock, your own breath. Let it be the only thing you follow for the whole sit. When another sound, an itch or a thought pulls at you, notice the pull, don't chase it, and come back to your one sound.
The Arthashastra's opening: indriya jaya, victory over the senses, which the book calls the whole of its science.
Hold onto this: the Arthashastra's opening, where the first kingdom to win is your own senses. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Indian traditions of kingship, in the Arthashastra and the epics alike, ask a ruler to master the senses; in the Arthashastra this is part of a prince's training in its first book, before any word on governing.

guess: an old ruling handbook's start: first, master your senses
an old law book's list of crimes a king must punish
a hymn sung when a new king is first given his crown

match.prompt: who was undone by what — tap the pairs.
pairs: ruined by desire for a brahmin's daughter
pride: wouldn't give back another's wife
wouldn't give his cousins their share

myth: conquering the senses means shutting them off completely
the text describes the senses not running wild: steered, not destroyed.
the Arthashastra uses Ravana and Duryodhana as warnings
both appear in its list of kings undone, next to Dandakya of the Bhoja line.
a big enough kingdom keeps an unmastered ruler safe
the text warns he soon perishes, even if he holds the whole earth.

fork.setup: you've just been made captain of your team. in week one, a teammate mouths off at you in front of everyone. by this chapter, what's your first move?
options: bench them on the spot, so everyone sees who's in charge.
notice the anger rising, and let it settle before you decide anything.
ignore it for good; a real captain never lets anything bother them.
fork.reveal: the Arthashastra puts the ruler's own anger first on the list of what to master. it doesn't say nothing should bother you; it says don't let the pull do the ruling.

original.note: Sanskrit indriyajaya, victory over the senses: the theme of Arthashastra 1.6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a book for kings would start with armies.
what it means: it says its whole science is victory over the senses, and it lists kings ruined by one pull each.
what a scholar hears: Arthashastra 1.6, the six to be given up (kama, krodha, lobha, mana, mada, harsha), with Dandakya, Ravana and Duryodhana among its examples.
recall: reasoned inquiry, the lamp of all sciences
teacher of the asuras, saluted first

chat.says: someone made a MEME of my campaign photo 💀 it's 1am and i'm drafting a clapback. thoughts
options: sleep on it. the book's first win is over your own anger, then the race.
post it now. a leader who doesn't hit back right away just looks weak.
delete every app. a real leader shuts out everything and feels nothing.
chat.meaning: The Arthashastra says its whole science is victory over the senses: anger steered, not obeyed, and not by switching yourself off.

Dandakya.meaning: a Bhoja king the text says was ruined by desire

Ravana.meaning: the demon king of Lanka in the Ramayana

Duryodhana.meaning: the eldest Kaurava prince in the Mahabharata

sources.ref: Arthashastra 1.6 (control of the senses: ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose with sound, touch, form, taste and smell; the whole science is the conquest of the senses; the six to give up; Dandakya, Ravana, Duryodhana among the kings undone)

notes: Arthashastra run, day 3. Merges the older drafts of 1586 and 1589, which both taught 1.6; vinaya and the elders (1.5) now sit on 1589.

Confirm in Arthashastra 1.6: the definition of control of the senses (ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose with sound, touch, form, taste and smell); 'this whole science is the conquest of the senses' (1.6.3); the six (kama, krodha, lobha, mana, mada, harsha; rendered desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, reckless glee) are listed but not counted in the voice; a king without control soon perishes though he hold the whole earth; Dandakya of the Bhoja line; Ravana (would not return another's wife) and Duryodhana (would not part with a portion of the kingdom), both under pride in common editions.
'The five doors of his own body' counts the five senses the text itself names.
Dandakya's gloss has no Devanagari on purpose (spelling not certain).
